projects.name: From missed signals to a useful follow-up
projects.summary: A live client workflow that turns newsletter activity and website enquiries into a shared contact record, timely alerts, and AI drafts the advisor reviews before sending.
projects.outcome: Live with a client; adoption and outcomes under evaluation

sections.title: The client problem
paragraphs: An independent real estate advisor had a newsletter audience and incoming website enquiries, but no shared view of what each person needed. Engagement lived in email reports, form details lived elsewhere, and relationship history depended on memory. A signal could be recorded without becoming a useful next action.

The client wanted individual follow-up without watching a dashboard or sending generic sequences. The system also had to preserve the existing email plan, leave website changes under the client’s control, and keep every contact email subject to human approval. This account reflects an early live review in October 2026; client and contact details are anonymized.

sections.title: Start with the existing workflow
paragraphs: I reviewed campaign activity and form submissions before designing the automation. The audit surfaced buying and selling interest already present in the data, as well as a form-to-email integration that passed an address but lost the context of the enquiry.
I brought the contact history into one Google Sheet owned by the client: one row per person, with their stated needs, relevant observations, and follow-up status.

sections.title: Separate interest from permission
paragraphs: The newsletter now includes a question with one-click answers for buying, selling, or watching the market. Declared answers and inferred interest are stored separately, so an interpretation is never presented as something the contact said.

Call recommendations require an explicit request. A later answer indicating that someone is only watching the market marks an earlier call request as “Don’t call.” Click activity on its own does not authorize a call.

sections.title: What is live
paragraphs: A Python watcher runs on Modal every 15 minutes. It reads Mailchimp campaign reports and website submissions through the Formspark API, updates the contact record, and sends the advisor an email alert with context and a draft follow-up. A weekly summary covers activity that does not need an immediate alert.

Reading forms directly preserves the enquiry, contact details, and preferred call time that the earlier integration dropped. Explicit call requests enter a call list with a next-business-day deadline. The system also checks whether a form submission reached the email list.

sections.title: Put guardrails around the draft
paragraphs: Claude, accessed through OpenRouter, drafts from the person’s history. Code checks each draft for prohibited references to browsing or click tracking, calls offered without a request, and writing rules. Rejected drafts are rewritten; a pre-checked fallback is available if validation still fails.

Observed browsing details stay in the advisor’s internal context and out of the outgoing draft. Scanner-like bursts of clicks are held instead of treated as genuine interest. The advisor reviews, edits, and sends every contact email; the system does not send outreach automatically.

sections.title: Make failure visible
paragraphs: The watcher retries temporary errors, protects against duplicate alerts, and records failures in the Sheet. An external heartbeat monitor flags a stopped schedule. Before client delivery, I tested real emails and clicks against a copy of the contact record, with alerts routed to a test inbox.

sections.title: Make the newsletter actionable
paragraphs: I built a newsletter template and a Claude Cowork workflow with checks for complete links and correct answer buttons. The new text-based newsletter format and question have been sent to the audience. Routine use of the builder remains part of the ongoing handoff.

sections.title: Early operation, measured carefully
paragraphs: At the October 2026 review, website enquiries reached the advisor as full alerts and contact records, including requests for calls. This demonstrates that existing demand is reaching the follow-up workflow; it does not establish that the system generated new demand.

At that point, the newsletter question had not produced genuine answers, call completion was not yet reliably recorded, and the client was not using the suggested drafts as-is. Conversion, revenue, and time saved remained unmeasured.

sections.title: What client feedback changed
paragraphs: Feedback showed that draft tone and contact-record usability needed more work. I separated subject lines from message text and added a compose-email link to reduce copying. Compatibility with the client’s usual email app is still being tested.

The next iteration will ground drafts in examples of what the advisor actually sends in each situation, improve the call-list workflow, and measure draft adoption and follow-through. Those are the next steps in this live engagement.

projects.name: A small team’s outbound engine
projects.summary: Seven stages, three LLM agents, and rules in code: do-not-contact checks at three stages, verification before send, and a human approval gate. Personalized outreach grew from about 10 to 150 messages per day.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: As a solo founder, researching accounts and writing relevant first messages competed with the time needed to build and deliver. I wanted more throughput while preserving account-specific context.

sections.title: What I built
paragraphs: I built a seven-stage Python pipeline covering lead scraping, enrichment, routing, personalized drafting, and upload to Instantly. Three LLM agents handle enrichment, routing, and drafting, calling Claude through OpenRouter. Apify and Google Sheets connect the research and operating workflow.
The cold-email infrastructure is part of this system: the value comes from connecting those stages into an end-to-end process.

sections.title: The checks around the model
paragraphs: Do-not-contact checks run at three stages. Email verification happens before sending, a cross-channel reply-stop prevents continued follow-up, and a human approval gate sits before messages ship. These controls live in the workflow and code.

sections.title: The result
paragraphs: Personalized outreach grew from roughly 10 to 150 messages per day in my own operation. Response quality, meetings, and revenue need their own measurement.
The system is designed to scale to 1,000+ personalized messages per day. That figure describes designed capacity; current operating volume is 150 per day.

projects.name: Infnty: AI for your work
projects.summary: A personalized AI newsletter in development: one shared editorial workflow, reader-specific application, relevant news, and human review before delivery.
projects.outcome: 20 early testers onboarded; beta under development

sections.title: The reader problem
paragraphs: A model announcement does not tell a consultant how to improve a research brief, or an analyst how to check a report. Useful AI guidance needs to connect to the work someone actually does, the tools they have, and the restrictions they work within.

Infnty is being developed as a weekly briefing built around one practical workflow. A shared editorial method provides the substance; personalization makes its application relevant to each reader. A small selection of AI news adds context for their work.

sections.title: My contribution
paragraphs: I’m a co-developer on Infnty. I designed the entire backend and delivery system for the personalized newsletter automation, including the path from reader profiles and editorial inputs to reviewed email output.
I’ve also onboarded 20 early testers and beta users. That is an onboarding milestone; sustained usage, retention, and improvements to readers’ work are still to be established.

sections.title: Keep the method intact
paragraphs: The human-written workflow package is the source of truth. It contains five executable steps, a copyable prompt, a populated worked example, checkpoints, failure modes, and guardrails. The system generates three to five representative previews for review before a workflow is approved. A content hash makes previous approvals stale when that workflow changes.

The application layer can adapt framing, use cases, tool fit, and explanation depth. Code preserves the approved workflow steps, base prompt, guardrails, and verified news facts when assembling the final content. This gives personalization a defined boundary.

sections.title: Match news to the reader
paragraphs: News discovery uses fixed editorial searches and a seven-day window. It does not receive reader profiles or audience-derived search terms. Candidates are deduplicated and must pass human verification before they enter the approved pool.

A separate relevance agent scores approved articles against each reader’s responsibilities, role, industry, tools, confidence, and restrictions. It does not receive the weekly workflow. Code selects three items from the stored scores and blocks generation if too few clear the relevance and restriction checks.

sections.title: Generate, check, then deliver
paragraphs: The TypeScript pipeline creates a personalization plan and structured content through OpenRouter. Deterministic checks validate schemas, required fields, source links, placeholders, and privacy-sensitive wording. An LLM critic provides a second review, with one revision attempt followed by revalidation.

Handlebars renders structured content into branded HTML. Google Sheets holds the operational records and review queue; n8n handles delivery. During the beta, every email requires human approval. Delivery checks subscription eligibility, consent, QA, scheduling, and the send ledger before SMTP.
The welcome email uses deterministic rendering to reflect the reader’s onboarding inputs and invite corrections. Generation, review, and delivery remain separate stages so each can be inspected.

sections.title: Learn from real use
paragraphs: Signed feedback links are designed to capture usefulness, saves, depth mismatch, and workflow attempts. An attempt is separate from a reported outcome on a real task. The tracking implementation includes event deduplication and suspicious-click handling, with the aim of learning whether readers actually use the workflows.

The core pipeline, templates, validation tests, and delivery workflow definitions are in place. Infnty remains under development while delivery readiness and the beta learning loop are validated. No productivity improvement, retention rate, or commercial result is claimed.

projects.name: Closing the lead-to-response gap
projects.summary: A B2B SaaS that sends automated SMS alerts for inbound real estate leads within five minutes, with failover logic.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: An inbound lead is only useful if someone notices it in time. LeadPulse focused on the handoff between a new enquiry and the agent who needs to respond.

sections.title: What I built
paragraphs: I built and shipped a B2B SaaS providing automated SMS lead alerts within five minutes, with failover logic. The system was designed around a clear operational action: get the lead in front of an agent.

sections.title: Beyond the happy path
paragraphs: Shipping included navigating Twilio A2P 10DLC registration and CASL requirements. Messaging infrastructure and the practical conditions for operating it were part of the product work.

sections.title: What this work demonstrates
paragraphs: A bounded product with a concrete user, a time-sensitive workflow, and delivery concerns beyond the UI. I’m describing the shipped capability here; adoption and conversion results are not yet part of the public case study.

projects.name: The content engine behind Clarity Works
projects.summary: A documented, seven-stage AI-assisted production line that connects one recording to published video, learning material, and repurposed content.
projects.outcome: Under 2 hours on a six-minute video

sections.title: The operational problem
paragraphs: Content was valuable, repeatable work with too many handoffs held in one person’s memory. As a solo founder, I needed a production process I could run consistently alongside the business.

sections.title: The production line
paragraphs: I documented seven gated stages, with a finished deliverable moving into the next step. A shared knowledge base keeps the output aligned with the business. Claude, Descript, and ElevenLabs support the work; recording and editorial judgment stay with me.

sections.title: What changed
paragraphs: The published proof asset reports moving from a 5+ hour manual baseline to under two hours from raw idea to upload for a six-minute video. It also records 16 published videos at the time that example was captured.

sections.title: More than one output
paragraphs: The same recording supports YouTube and the Sprint pre-watch library, with a repurposing stage for other channels. The full walkthrough is public, so the workflow can be inspected alongside the claim.

projects.name: Building AI capability that stays with the team
projects.summary: A workflow-first advisory method: understand the business, diagnose the work, improve the SOP, then build with the team.
projects.outcome: A structured method, teaching assets, and handoff

sections.title: The problem I work on
paragraphs: New tools do not resolve an unclear process. I started Clarity Works around a practical question: how can a non-technical team learn to improve its own work with AI?

sections.title: The method
paragraphs: The operating sequence is context, diagnosis, SOP, and build. I use it to turn business goals and scattered tasks into a clear workflow, then help the team build the AI-assisted version. Capability transfer runs through the engagement.

sections.title: How I package it
paragraphs: The 30-day Sprint is designed around one improved SOP, one useful workflow, and a roadmap for the next opportunities. The phased Partner Program extends the method across core operations, with documentation, ownership, and review habits. These are the programs’ intended deliverables.

sections.title: Teaching in the open
paragraphs: I publish the frameworks on YouTube and use those materials as pre-work. Live sessions can then focus on the client’s actual process, decisions, and build.

notes.title: The SOP is part of the architecture
notes.summary: Before choosing the agent, understand the decisions, handoffs, and exceptions in the work.
paragraphs: When a team asks for an AI workflow, my first question is about the work itself. What starts it? Who makes the decision? What information do they need? Where does the process stall?

Those questions are architectural. A model can help interpret an input, but the surrounding workflow still needs clear ownership, inputs, outputs, and a useful next action. An undocumented process makes those decisions harder to see.

That is why workflow mapping and SOP improvement come before the assisted build in the AI Capability Ladder I use at Clarity Works. The process gives the build its shape. It also gives the team something concrete to question and improve.

I want a working session to leave behind more than a promising demo. The team should be able to explain what the workflow does, recognize when it needs human judgment, and maintain the process as the work changes.
For me, discovery and engineering belong in the same conversation. Understanding the process is how I decide what is worth building.

notes.title: Build the checks around the model
notes.summary: What my outbound pipeline taught me about putting operational rules in code.
paragraphs: My outbound pipeline uses three LLM agents for enrichment, routing, and drafting. Those are useful places for contextual reasoning. The operating rules around them need a different treatment.

A do-not-contact record needs to stop the workflow. A reply needs to stop follow-up. An unverified email needs to be checked before sending. These rules should be explicit in the system that runs the work.

In the pipeline, do-not-contact checks run at three stages, verification happens before send, and a cross-channel reply-stop prevents continued follow-up. There is also a human approval gate before a message ships.
The distinction shapes how I think about applied AI: use the model where interpretation helps, and make the boundaries around its output inspectable. A well-written prompt is one part of that design.

The result I can point to today is throughput: personalized outreach grew from about 10 to 150 messages a day. To tell the full business story, response quality and downstream outcomes need their own measurement.

about.lead: My economics background made me curious about incentives and ownership. Building AI systems made that practical.
paragraphs: I founded Clarity Works to help service-based businesses build AI capability inside their teams. I work from business context to workflow diagnosis, SOP improvement, and the first useful AI-assisted build.

That same method shapes my work: a live client follow-up system, my outbound engine, and the content pipeline behind my educational work. I publish the frameworks openly and use real builds to explain the decisions.

I build with Claude Code and Codex, work with Python and SQL, and have foundational TypeScript experience. I care about understanding the logic, making failure modes visible, and leaving a workflow people can maintain.
